newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK governor slams accusers of cover-up in scandal.
newsitem.headline: HK governor slams accusers of cover-up in scandal.

text.p: Hong Kong's Governor Chris Patten, grappling with a growing scandal, hit back furiously on Thursday at critics who suggested his government had covered up why it ousted its immigration chief last July.
But many politicians and analysts were convinced the full story had yet to be told about why former immigration director Laurence Leung was forced out.

The government says it asked him to go because he failed to disclose business ties as required under the rules, and it dismissed as groundless speculation that Leung -- in a job particularly sensitive in the runup to Hong Kong's handover to China on July 1 this year -- had spied for Beijing.

Legislators say questions remain unanswered, such as who ordered an anti-corruption probe against Leung, why this was done, and whether or not other official reports exist showing he was a security threat.
"I think there has been a lot of self-indulgent nonsense written and said about this case," a steaming Patten told reporters at the airport after returning from London.
He said it was unacceptable for senior officials with questionable integrity to serve in his administration.
Patten also said he was amazed there had been suggestions the misdeeds that the government had found Leung to have committed deserved only a slap on the wrist.

"If you had discovered that the director of the immigration service couldn't pass an integrity check but that the government had swept it under the carpet and let him stay in office, you would have pilloried the governmment, and rightly," he said.

Patten praised Lam Woon-kwong, the government's personnel chief responsible for removing Leung, as a man of integrity and a "bulwark between Hong Kong being successful and Hong Kong declining into sleaze and cronyism".
But political commentators said the issue was no longer merely restricted to any sins of Leung -- that the government's own credibility was now on trial.
"Suspicion of a political cover-up in the espisode remains considerable," wrote analyst Chris Yeung in the South China Morning Post newspaper.
China's top official for Hong Kong affairs, Lu Ping, called on the territory's government to take steps to prevent the civil service's credibility being affected by the controversy.

"I hope the Hong Kong government or the Legislative Council (legislature) will take appropriate action so that the credibility of Hong Kong's civil service will not be affected," the head of the Hong Kong and Macau Affairs Office told reporters in Beijing.
Leung's sudden early retirement for "personal reasons" last July caused an uproar in the territory.
British press reports alleged he had been spying for China, to whom the colony reverts at midnight on June 30. Leung has denied being a spy.
Patten was not asked about this at his brief airport session with reporters, but both he and Lam have said this week there was no security breach at the Immigration Department.
Leung was responsible for areas such as issuing of passports and visas, immigration and border controls, and was privy to sensitive information in handover talks with China.
Local politicans were not happy with Patten's denial of a cover-up and urged the government to reveal the whole truth.
"We still have our doubts about whether that is the real reason for asking Laurence Leung to leave," Liberal Party leader Allen Lee told the government on Thursday.
"It seems the penalty for his not reporting his dealings or business affairs is quite severe. The government could issue a warning... Nevertheless, is that the real reason?" Lee asked.

Last Friday, Leung told the Hong Kong parliamentary inquiry into his sudden departure that he had been forced to quit, contradicting his own and the government's initial stance that he retired for personal reasons.

An anti-corruption probe showed Leung had undisclosed shareholdings, had a business relationship with a legislator, had invested in a mainland Chinese enterprise and had failed to repay a government housing loan promptly, Lam said.
